label: GPT-6 Luna
output:
Nana,

I wish I could be there with you and Aunt Denise in the kitchen tonight. I’ve been trying to write this all week, and every time I start, I get choked up and close the laptop. So I’m going to stop trying to find the perfect words and just tell you what I want you to know.

I’m sorry I can’t be there for the move tomorrow. I’m primary on call all week, and I couldn’t find anyone to swap with me. I know you’ve told me it’s okay, and everyone else has too. I believe you. I’m still sorry I’ll miss this moment, though. I wish I could help carry a box, make a dozen trips to the car, and then sit with you for a while after it’s all done.

Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street. That’s a lot of life in one house. It’s where Grandpa Walt was, and where half the family seemed to grow up around your kitchen table. When I think of the house, I don’t really think of the walls or the furniture. I think of you in it. The kitchen, the back steps, the sound of the cuckoo clock, and you making room for whoever showed up hungry or needing a place to land. The house meant so much to me because you were there.

Some of my happiest memories are those summers when I was a kid and staying over. You’d let me stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays on that little TV in the kitchen—as long as I dried the dishes. I don’t remember how good I was at drying dishes, but I remember thinking that staying up late with you and the game was the best deal in the world.

You taught me crib at seven, and you never once let me win. I’m still not sure if that was good teaching or just a very long campaign to keep me humble. When I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I knew I’d won something special, but I didn’t realize the prize would be so good. I’m not saying the butter tarts were payment, but I’m also not saying they weren’t.

I think about your back steps, too. You’d be out there with your tea at six in the morning, and I’d come sit with you. You never said much until you’d finished your cup. I didn’t know then how much I’d value those quiet mornings. I do now. There was something lovely about being with you without needing to fill every minute with words.

And I’ve never forgotten the card you sent when I got my job in Toronto. There was a twenty-dollar bill taped inside, and your note said, “for pizza, you look thin on the computer.” You were looking out for me from a distance, in the most Nana way possible. I still laugh when I think about it—and I can confirm that the pizza budget helped.

Last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner, you asked if the internet was broken again and if I’d fixed it. Now you ask me every time, “Did anything break?” It’s become one of my favourite questions. For the record, things do break, but I usually get them sorted. And now I have to admit that, thanks to you, I’ll probably hear your voice asking that question in my head every time my phone rings.

Tomorrow is a big change, and I know it may feel strange to leave the house after all those years. I also know Elmwood Terrace looks nice, you chose it for yourself, and you’re excited about what comes next. I’m proud of you for making this decision yourself. Nobody made you do it. You looked at what you wanted, decided what was right for you, and took the next step. That takes courage, and I hope you know how much I admire it.

I’m glad they have a crib league there. I’m also a little suspicious that you’ve chosen a place with an official league because you’re hoping to find new people to beat. Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I’m getting the crib board. That seems fair to me—though I imagine you’ll still have plenty of opportunities to teach me a lesson at the table.

I can picture your new room on the second floor, looking out at the parking lot and that big maple. Maybe in the morning you’ll have your tea and watch the day get going. It won’t be the back steps on Kathleen Street, but you’ll bring the important part with you: the way you make a place feel like home.

I’ll be up the weekend of December 5, once my rotation is done. I can’t wait to see you, hear how you’re settling in, and play the first game on the crib board at the new place. I expect you to play honestly. I also expect you to try to win, because I know you wouldn’t have it any other way.

Nana, I love you. Thank you for all the summers, all the games, all the food, all the quiet mornings, and all the ways you’ve looked after me—even from a distance. Kathleen Street will always mean a lot to me, but what made it special was you. And you’re not leaving that behind.

I’ll see you on December 5. Save me a seat, and maybe go easy on me for the first hand.

Love you,

[Your name]
